statements.text: Generative artificial intelligence isn’t a trend; it’s the backbone of the next industrial era. Countries around the globe are racing to build the full AI stack: data centers, chips, power, and platforms. Here in the United States, we must ensure that we have the right policies in place to have enough energy to power AI and make America an attractive place to build the entire AI supply chain.
statements.venue: Latta press release on subcommittee markup of his AI energy bills

statements.text: America’s adversaries are not waiting for us to figure this out. If AI can find serious vulnerabilities in widely used software, China and other bad actors will look for ways to use similar tools against us. We need to make sure trusted American defenders have the coordination, access, and support required to stay ahead.
statements.venue: Press release on bipartisan letter to National Cyber Director

statements.text: There is no one-size-fits-all approach to regulating this technology, nor should there be. To unlock the full potential of AI, we must establish foundational protection for the data that powers many of these new AI tools by enacting a comprehensive data privacy standard in the United States.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, E&C subcommittee hearing 'Leveraging AI to Enhance American Communications'

statements.text: In the same way humans are not perfect, AI is not perfect, either. Because humans design AI algorithms, AI systems may contain unintentional bias, which unfortunately could lead to discrimination.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, E&C subcommittee hearing 'Leveraging AI to Enhance American Communications'

statements.text: we are talking about all the AI, and one of the things—of course, we have had a lot of questions about, in the past, about how algorithms are set, especially when we are talking about AI. How would you make sure that those algorithms are correct, that they are not biased to one side or the other?
statements.context: Rep. Latta poses a question to a witness during a congressional event on innovation in Congress.

statements.text: I want to be an AI contrarian because I think it can do tremendous things for communications. That if we introduce machine learning and pattern recognition on our wired and wireless networks, we are going to be able to radically increase our efficiency.
statements.context: Exchange during a House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology oversight hearing on the FCC, where Rep. Walberg asks the FCC commissioners how the agency is approaching AI in telecommunications.

statements.text: The amount of power we're going to have to have — we're not even close right now
statements.venue: Axios, remarks on planned hearing on AI power use

statements.text: And one of the things I know that we have talked about in the past is about permitting, and we got to get it done. [...] But could you talk briefly about if we don't win this race, what is going to happen, especially if we don't get our permitting done in this committee and in the House?
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI applications, where a member questions a witness about U.S.-China AI investment and domestic permitting.

statements.text: All the while, we are in the midst of a critical race to lead the world in AI development. The stakes could not be higher [...] I am encouraged that your Department has been rightly focused on the energy needs of our growing AI industry and why it is so important for our Nation and the world for the United States to win.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Bob Latta, chair of the Energy Subcommittee, at a House hearing on the DOE FY2026 budget with Secretary Chris Wright.

statements.text: This legislation will require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish a pilot program to explore the use of artificial intelligence in support of its product safety efforts.
statements.context: Floor remarks in the U.S. House of Representatives advocating passage of H.R. 1770, the Consumer Safety Technology Act.

statements.text: Mr. Speaker, I move to suspend the rules and pass the bill (H.R. 1770) to direct the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish a pilot program to explore the use of artificial intelligence in support of the mission of the Commission and to direct the Secretary of Commerce and the Federal Trade Commission to study and report on the use of blockchain technology and tokens, respectively.
statements.context: Floor of the U.S. House of Representatives during consideration of H.R. 1770, the Consumer Safety Technology Act.

statements.text: On my committees, we also look at how you’re going to power AI, like with data centers. We have to make sure we have proper guardrails on it. People will say that we shouldn’t have any AI, well, that’s not going to happen. AI is going to be a huge driver of our economy.

Throughout Congress, we spend a lot of time talking about U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. [...] The national security issues with AI and adversarial nations like China and having whose values control AI is vitally important. [...] we beat China in the race to AI.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI and electric grid power demand.

statements.text: The ability of malign actors like Russia and Communist China using AI models to disrupt global economies are no longer theoretical, but a reality. [...] Many question whether AI, and the data centers that power it, will ultimately do more harm than good, particularly when it comes to individual energy costs. These concerns deserve to be taken seriously.
statements.context: Opening statement by the Chairman of the House Energy Subcommittee at a legislative hearing on AI's impact on power-grid demand.

statements.text: Access to reliable and affordable energy is the linchpin to U.S. leadership in AI development. [...] From that work, it is safe to assume AI is one of the defining challenges of our time. It encompasses the race for economic strength, technological leadership, and national security in the 21st century.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Energy Subcommittee hearing 'AI and the Grid'

statements.text: At the same time, the American people are understandably uneasy. Many question whether AI, and the data centers that power it, will ultimately do more harm than good, particularly when it comes to individual energy costs. These concerns deserve to be taken seriously.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Energy Subcommittee hearing 'AI and the Grid'

statements.text: Our global competitors are not slowing down. China is investing heavily in AI with the explicit goal of surpassing the United States.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Energy Subcommittee hearing 'AI and the Grid'

statements.text: Protecting the American people means ensuring the systems they rely on every day, including our hospitals, water systems, and electric grid, remain safe, secure, and reliable. Our adversaries are constantly looking for new ways to target our critical infrastructure, and we must make sure we are prepared to respond.
statements.venue: Press release on Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act
